blocks.text: A farmer in Jos whose maize will not thrive tests his soil and finds a pH of 4.5. He spreads lime, retests, and gets 6.5. Two numbers told him exactly what was wrong and how much to add. The pH scale turns a vague idea of sourness into something you can measure and act on.

blocks.title: pH
blocks.text: pH is the negative logarithm to base ten of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/dm3. That is pH = -log10[H+]. The scale normally runs from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral at 25 degrees Celsius, below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline.

blocks.caption: The two forms of the pH relationship

blocks.markdown:
## Reading the scale

Because the scale is logarithmic, **each whole unit represents a tenfold change** in hydrogen ion concentration. A solution of pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one of pH 4 and a hundred times more acidic than one of pH 5.

A useful shortcut: for a strong monobasic acid such as HCl, the acid ionises completely, so the hydrogen ion concentration equals the acid concentration.

- 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl gives [H+] = 10^-1, so pH = 1
- 0.01 mol/dm3 HCl gives [H+] = 10^-2, so pH = 2
- 0.001 mol/dm3 HCl gives [H+] = 10^-3, so pH = 3

blocks.caption: Common acid-base indicators and their colour changes

blocks.title: Finding pH from concentration
blocks.prompt: Calculate the pH of a 0.01 mol/dm3 solution of hydrochloric acid, and state what happens to the pH if the solution is diluted ten times.

steps.text: Hydrochloric acid is a strong monobasic acid, so it ionises completely and every mole of HCl gives one mole of H+.
Therefore [H+] = 0.01 mol/dm3, which can be written as 1 x 10^-2 mol/dm3.
Diluting ten times reduces [H+] from 10^-2 to 10^-3 mol/dm3.
The new pH is -log10(10^-3) = 3, so the pH rises by exactly one unit.
Note that diluting an acid raises its pH towards 7 but can never push it past 7, because water itself is neutral.

blocks.answer: pH = 2; after a tenfold dilution the pH becomes 3

blocks.markdown:
## Choosing an indicator for a titration

An indicator is itself a weak acid whose ionised and un-ionised forms differ in colour. It changes colour only over a narrow pH range, so it must be chosen so that this range falls within the sharp pH jump at the end point of the particular titration.

| Titration | Salt formed | pH at equivalence | Suitable indicator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strong acid + strong alkali | Neutral | 7 | Methyl orange or phenolphthalein |
| Strong acid + weak base | Acidic | Below 7 | Methyl orange |
| Weak acid + strong alkali | Alkaline | Above 7 | Phenolphthalein |
| Weak acid + weak base | Varies | No sharp jump | No suitable indicator |

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Methyl orange changes in the acidic range, so use it when the salt formed is acidic. Phenolphthalein changes in the alkaline range, so use it when the salt formed is alkaline. Either works when the salt is neutral.

blocks.title: Two common slips
blocks.text: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid, not white or clear-with-a-tinge: write colourless. And a pH of 0 does not mean 'no acidity' — it means a hydrogen ion concentration of 1 mol/dm3, which is extremely acidic.

points: pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/dm3.
Each pH unit represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
For a strong monobasic acid the hydrogen ion concentration equals the acid concentration.
Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.
Choose methyl orange when the salt formed is acidic and phenolphthalein when it is alkaline.
